party.description: The New Zealand National Party (Rōpū Nāhinara) is a centre-right conservative party. It was founded in 1936 as a merger between the liberal United party and conservative Reform parties, its programmes have emphasised the incremental reduction in the role of government to support business and encourage growth. It currently leads the government with 49 seats in parliament. National has historically been regarded as the ‘natural party of government.’ Having been dominant throughout the 20th century.  It has led the government 6 times and held office for longer than Labour. Christopher Luxon is the current leader, with a 2026 slogan of “Fixing the Basics, Building the Future.”

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that Rolleston is a well-placed hub for moving goods around, as it is on State Highway 1, the main southern train line, and connected by road and rail to the West Coast. Because many agricultural goods are moved through this area, making it easier to move goods between trains and trucks will increase efficiency and economic opportunity for producers in this area.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would invest $50m in a road and rail "intermodal hub" in Rolleston. This funding would be dependent on the result of a business case, where private freight companies and customers would also invest in the hub. It would only go ahead with a mix of public and private funding.  This party estimates that this policy would cost $50m.

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that Queenstown is growing fast and there is a lot of traffic on the section of road between Hansen Road down to the Five Mile roundabout. This party says this road should be wider, as it carries freight, tourists and workers. The gondola, which reduces traffic as well as being a tourist attraction and the local government should receive funding for it as public transport.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would commit $25m to increasing the section of State Highway 6 in Queenstown to four lanes. It would also ensure that the Queenstown gondola could access money from the National Land Transport Fund as a public transport service.

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that the South Island is particularly vulnerable to failures in transport networks, particularly given its reliance on several bridges. Earthquakes, flooding, spread-out communities, big rivers and mountains all mean roads and bridges can easily be damaged and communities could face long detours or have no way to get around. Focusing government money on improving the most at-risk parts of the network could make the South Island transport network more resilient.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would use the next government policy statement on transport to prioritise the South Island road network's most important points, especially state highway bridges.

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that the Crown owns 1.2 million hectares of land through the South Island, which is leased to farmers for pastoral grazing. Much of this land is at higher elevations. Farmers need certainty about which kinds of activities they can do on this land without requiring consent. Giving farmers other income sources on this land, like beekeeping or horticulture, would provide farmers with the confidence to invest and diversify.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would pass a law implementing changed policy settings for the kinds of activity to be carried out on Crown pastoral land, and for when farmers need approval or consent for activities.

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that international tourists are key parts of the economy, especially those who want to see natural attractions. These are managed by the Department of Conservation, and while New Zealanders could continue accessing them for free, tourists should pay some costs towards the upkeep. This money would be invested into tourist infrastructure at these locations.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would charge international visitors for access to a handful of key NZ attractions from 2027. This money would be largely reinvested in tourist infrastructure and conservation efforts in these areas. This is expected to raise $60 million per year.

Changing planning rules for town centres would make it easier to convert spaces into new businesses or accommodation. This would especially help places where businesses want to cater to a growing tourist sector.

attributes.value: This party says that tourism on conservation land is important to the New Zealand economy. More businesses should be able to receive concessions for operations on conservation land, and these concessions should be faster and simpler. This will create jobs and encourage tourists. Currently, around 1,600 businesses operate on conservation land, with revenue around $5.3m each year.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would remove some rules around concessions on conservation land, so 30-40 percent of applications could be processed automatically. Regional performance metrics would calculate how these concessions are granted and how long it takes.

attributes.value: This party says that rocks from quarrying are useful on farms for tracks and maintenance, but it can be complicated to get consent for this quarrying. Gravel in riverbeds can be used for aggregate, and removing gravel can reduce flood impacts. In the legislation replacing the RMA, consistent rules for this activity will be applied throughout the country.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would create a National Standard for on-farm quarrying and gravel removal from rivers in the legislation replacing the RMA. This would cut consents for farmers and provide sources of gravel and rock.

Gold export revenues have nearly tripled in the last three years to $1.8bn. Mining projects in the South Island were included in the government's Fast-track approvals law, and a policy statement for mining specifically would emphasise that these projects are important to national exports.

attributes.value: This party says that data centres are a growing industry well-suited to setting up in NZ, especially the South Island with its cool climate. However, data centres also use a lot of electricity, which could drive up prices for households and businesses. Making sure that data centres are only built when new electricity generation will also be built would give data centres and electricity generators security without making power prices more expensive.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would only approve new data centres when these are accompanied by new, firm generation.

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that trained and certified service dogs support people with disabilities including blindness and low vision, epilepsy and hearing loss. These animals have the right to access all public places but are sometimes turned away because they are assumed to be pets. An ID card for these animals will ensure that the dogs and their owners can show they have the right to access public places.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would issue a standardised national card for all owners of certified service dogs. This would make it clear to businesses and other operators that these animals and their owners have the right to be in public places, and would distinguish them from other animals and pets which do not have the same rights.

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that responsibilities for introduced animals are shared between different agencies, which can make management unclear. Species which hunters and anglers appreciate, like trout and deer, are seen only as pests rather than natural resources. Introduced animals should not be seen as pests by default, especially when they are valued for their cultural, economic or caloric potential. It is possible to balance protecting native species and environments and retaining deer to hunt.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would replace the current "Tahr Control Plan" and seek proposals to recognise further "Herds of Special Interest". Introduced species would be recognised in the law, not just as pests.

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that the Game Council and Fish and Game are run by hunters and anglers, who should take the lead in managing introduced species in their areas. These organisations need a clearly defined role for managing Herds of Special Interest and coordinating access for hunters on conservation land

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would make the Game Council the statutory manager of introduced game animals in NZ. It would also be responsible for managing access for hunting on conservation land and negotiating between the needs of different users. The legislation for Fish and Game New Zealand would be reformed, directing more resources to habitats, accountability for licence holders and simplifying administration.

attributes.value: This party says that hunting can contribute to the economy. People want to come to New Zealand to hunt animals like tahr which cannot be hunted elsewhere. Jobs like taxidermy, guides and helicopters are supported by people hunting. Increasing the number of people coming to New Zealand to hunt will be good for the economy.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would promote tourism for guided hunting in overseas markets. It would simplify the process of shipping a taxidermied trophy animal outside of the country, including working on customs processes and veterinary certification. It would develop further rules around different types of hunting: recreational, commercial, guided, and aerial.

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that accessing the outdoors is important for hunting to take place. The current government has created an access charter for recreational hunting and fishing. This party wants to continue that work by adding more hunting-interest groups to the charter and making more Crown-owned land accessible for hunting and fishing.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would add the Game Animal Council, Overseas Investment Office and Land Information NZ to the Access Charter. Access for hunters would be protected when land is purchased by overseas investors if possible.

attributes.value: This party would pursue trade deals with Brazil, Switzerland, Argentina, Bangladesh, Nigeria, Uruguay and the European Free Trade Association (Iceland, Liechtenstein and Norway). Negotiations with these countries would begin in the next five years. When deals were signed, a second set of deals with South Africa, Turkey, Colombia, Morocco, Sri Lanka and Mauritius would be the next focus.

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that exports help grow NZ's economy, increasing jobs and wages. If businesses are selling more outside of NZ, more money will return to local communities. Exports have increased from $94.4bn to $114.1bn over the current term of government, and that trajectory should continue.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would continue to support a goal of doubling NZ's export earnings by 2034. This would be done by carrying out at least 23 trade missions in the next term of government, procuring deals with 13 countries identified as candidates for trade agreements, and by securing agreements for supplying essential goods like oil. Digital customs and trade processes would eliminate barriers to trade, and New Zealand Trade and Enterprise would have a sharper mandate to develop export growth.

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that people who live in rural NZ should be able to access health care without travelling a long way. Ultrasounds are useful diagnostic tools, and giving rural-based clinicians the ability to use them will make it easier to decide whether they can be treated locally or need hospital care. Currently, 29% of rural clinicians are paying for PRIME emergency response training themselves; government funding for this program could make it easier for rural health professionals to respond to emergencies.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would invest $2.5m in a ultrasound training programmed called POCUS, aimed at rural doctors and nurses who carry out after-hours care and provide additional funding for rural clinicians to receive PRIME emergency response training. This would train 140 health professionals in ultrasounds and 150 people in emergency response. To increase the workforce in rural health practices, a $6m investment would help rural general practices to get more staff.  This party estimates that this policy would cost $8.5m.

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that teachers arrive in schools without classroom experience, impacting learning. The current government has created the Schools Onsite Training Programme so teachers can receive a stipend to spend three days a week in classrooms while training.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would increase the number of places in the Schools Onsite Training Programme to 704 each year by 2028, focusing on subjects and areas with teacher shortages. It would also add 50 places to the Teacher Bonding Scheme, bringing the total to 235, which is aimed at helping schools with staffing challenges to attract more staff.

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that parents need more flexibility for taking leave, including taking paid leave at the same time as their partner, so they can receive more support if needed. Current arrangements create financial penalties for people who take time off work to care for their children. Both parents should have the opportunity to access parental leave if they choose.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would increase parental leave to 27 weeks in the 2027 budget, with further increases in 2028 and 2029. This leave could be split between parents or shared in overlapping periods. After returning to work, pay for annual leave would be calculated based on yearly salaries, rather than average pay for parents who have earned less due to taking parental leave. This party would also continue contributing to a parent's Kiwisaver while they take paid parental leave. Eventually, this party would aim to increase paid parental leave to 40 weeks.

attributes.value: This party says that the existing Harbour Bridge in Auckland is a busy corridor, which is needed for $1b of economic activity. This is projected to increase to $3.9b by 2051. Making it easier to get to central Auckland from the north would be good for productivity and increase economic activity. Bridges and tunnels have both been proposed, but detailed information about this project is needed before the government spends billions of dollars on it.

attributes.value: This party would fund an independent detailed business case of the second Waitematā crossing, led by someone who reports to the ministers for finance, transport, Auckland and cabinet as a whole. Consultation with other major parties will ensure that funding for this project can endure across terms of government.

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that in contexts like apartments or for renters it isn't possible to install traditional solar panels, but small solar set-ups on balconies are an option. After a review found that these systems are safe, this party says that making the regulations for small solar set-ups in NZ simpler will improve reliability and affordability for people. Countries like Germany already have similar rules, which this party says is proof they will work in New Zealand.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would follow the recommendations in the solar regulatory review, to reduce the number of approvals needed for new solar set-ups. It would allow more installers to carry out inspections and making approval times for lines companies shorter, and estimates that the net benefits would be between $28 million and $50 million over 10 years.  This party estimates that this policy would cost $28 million and $50 million over 10 years.

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that that previous clean vehicle standards did not strike the balance between emission reductions and affordability, meaning cars were expensive. The current government made short-term changes to make cars cheaper. This party wants to continue a full review of the Clean Vehicle standards, ensuring used cars should be held to a different standard than new vehicles.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would retain the current Clean Vehicle Standards as a review continues. It would set different emission targets for imported used vehicles compared to new vehicles. It would also work with the vehicle industry to ensure the standards work for importers and create target settings to take effect in January 2028.

attributes.value: This party says that that it is focused on growing the economy and do not want to introduce new taxes. It does not want to make commitments that would involving adding or increasing taxes for any New Zealanders. It says it can invest in government services without changing any parameters on the tax system.

attributes.name: How

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that Kiwisaver is a way for people to build up money for themselves during retirement, and everyone who is working should be part of it. The money in Kiwisaver is also important for providing capital for investments in New Zealand's future, like major projects or infrastructure. Contributions from the government for babies who are automatically enrolled will help the investment grow over time.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would make Kiwisaver compulsory from July 2028 and life combined contribution rates (individuals and employers) to 12% by 2032. For babies, it would contribute a $1500 "Baby Boost" payment to all New Zealanders at birth, automatically enrolling them in Kiwisaver. It would also make other changes to Kiwisaver, including government contributions through paid parental leave and requiring employers to maintain payments for people over the age of 65 who are still working.

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that NZ needs to grow its housing stock and infrastructure, and the Fast-track planning laws have made it easier for new housing to be built. However, some councils are concerned that there is not appropriate infrastructure, like roads and water systems, to support these new developments. To make it easier for councils, the costs of this new infrastructure should be easy to recover when a new project is approved.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would allow councils to amend their "Development Contribution" policies to recover costs from new developments, including in the six months after an application is granted, rather than costs being locked in at the time of application. For projects in multiple council areas, there would be a mechanism to calculate costs for different territorial authorities. Over time, this system would be replaced with "Development Levies" which would be in place by 2029.

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that New Zealanders should keep more money, rather than paying taxes, to save money for their own future. Taking home more pay and repaying a student loan over a longer period will give graduates more options for how to spend their money. People who have been educated in New Zealand and are staying to work here should have more money available while starting their careers.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would reduce the annual repayment rate for student loans to 10 percent, from the current rate of 12 percent. Student loans for people in NZ would remain interest-free. People could continue to make additional repayments if they wished. Currently, there are $16.8bn of student loans owed to the government. Because of a slower rate of repayment, this party would write off $283m of student loans in the 2026/27 financial year to make up the loss in value from the interest-free loans.

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that many New Zealanders receive a heavily subsidised education, but do not use their skills in NZ. To support people to stay in New Zealand, overseas-based student loan holders who are not making repayments need to be penalised. The Inland Revenue Department (IRD) already has some tools, like charging interest to overseas-based loan holders and monitoring the border for people who have not paid their student loans. More penalties and limits for people who are not paying their student loans would recover more money.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value:
This party would add another 1 percent of interest for overseas student loan holders. For overseas-based New Zealanders withdrawing their Kiwisaver under the "permanent migration" category, money from Kiwisaver would clear the remaining student loan debt first. IRD would receive $10m of additional funding for student loan recovery and be allowed to register a charge for recovery in another country without getting a court order. attributes.value: This party says that 1 in 3 children between the ages of 13-17 spends more than 5 hours on social media every day. Restricting social media use will give parents and teachers more options to look after teenagers and create positive behavioural shifts.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would pass a bill requiring that companies including Instagram, TikTok, Facebook and Snapchat check the age of all users to make sure they are not under 16. These companies would be required to regularly report on risks to children on their platforms, and an online safety regulator would monitor compliance. AI companies and other new technologies would be included in the framework, and platforms which fail to take these measures will be fined, based on a percentage of their annual global revenue.

attributes.value: This party would limit council rate rises to between 2 and 4 percent per year. Every 6 years, this target range would be reviewed and adapted if necessary. In exceptional circumstances, councils could apply for an exemption by demonstrating their financial management or to recover from an unpredictable event like a natural disaster. An independent regulator would monitor and advise councils and the government on the rates target. The caps would take effect from 1 July 2029.

The tax, which has been frozen since 2020, is important for funding road infrastructure. With the conflict in Iran making fuel more expensive, fuel tax and road user charge increases can be delayed a year, until 2028.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would cancel the planned 12c increase to the fuel excise tax in 2027. Instead, the party would increase the fuel excise tax in 2028, rising by 5c at 6 month intervals until 2030. At that point, annual 5c increases would resume. Because the excise tax goes into the National Land Transport Fund for road maintenance and creation, it would make up the shortfall with money from other parts of the government.

attributes.value: This party says that that the Kiwisaver policy was designed with urban housing in mind. This means that people working on farms have to wait longer to buy property. Similarly, Kiwisaver withdrawals cannot be used for purchasing a farm through a company. This change will allow people to buy their first farms with less debt.

If they are buying a farm where they are the majority owner, and will be living on the farm, regardless of whether the ownership structure is a partnership, a trust, a company or individuals, they will be eligible to withdraw their Kiwisaver for this purchase too.

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that councils create the infrastructure tourists use and deserve a direct financial benefit for hosting visitors, who also put pressure on local resources. Distributing the international visitor levy money not committed to the Department of Conservation and a tourism growth fund to councils is an alternative to a bed tax, which would disproportionately affect domestic tourists in New Zealand. This would also give councils money sooner than the time it would take to set up a bed fee. This is an alternative to raising taxes, which this party opposes.

attributes.value: This party would distribute $100m of the International Visitor Levy to DOC and $50m to a Tourism Priorities fund each year. The rest of the money, an estimated $385m over the first four years, would be distributed to councils, determined as a share of how many international visitors spend the night in their areas. This party would also commit to keeping the levy at the current amount for the next three years, to provide certainty to the tourism industry. As tourist numbers grow, the amount given to councils is expected to increase.

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that a home is an essential way for New Zealanders to build wealth. The First Home Loan scheme has operated since 2003, allowing people to purchase their first homes with a 5% deposit, instead of a standard 20% deposit. However, some people who are struggling to afford the deposit on their first home fall above the income cap of $95,000 for a person buying alone and $150,000 for two people buying together (both with no dependents). Raising the eligibility criteria will mean more people can buy homes with low deposits. Raising and simplifying the eligibility will allow more people to buy houses.

attributes.value: This party would raise the eligibility so anyone earning less than $300,000 per year, whether single or a couple, could access the 5% deposit of the First Home Loan scheme. These lower deposits would only apply to people purchasing their first property. The loans would be approved by banks, as already happens, meaning no-one would be issued with a loan they cannot afford. The fiscal impact of this policy is expected to be between $4m-$6m.

attributes.value: This party says that home energy tools like solar power and batteries lower household power bills and provide resilience in the energy system. With a high cost of living, this would help people finding it hard to pay power bills.

attributes.value: This party would launch the Home Energy Fund, jointly owned by central government and participating councils. The fund would pay a approved installer to add batteries or solar panels to a home and then property owner would repay the fund at low interest rates over a ten-year period. The loans would be secured against the value of the property, and available to ratepayers with at least 20% equity in their property. The loans could be used for solar installation, batteries, heat pumps, insulation and other developments to make homes more efficient.

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that NZ law does not define what consent is, but instead says what consent is not. This means that for legal purposes, the absence of a person saying "no" can be considered consent, depending on the circumstance. To create a better system for the victims of sexual offending, and to be in line with other jurisdictions, the definition of consent should be specified in the law.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would amend the Crimes Act to specify that consent must be actively given, whether through words or actions. Consent is also not permanent; consent given at one point in time, for one action, is not consent for all future actions. The prosecution would still need to prove beyond reasonable doubt that consent wasn't given, and that the defendant didn't believe, on reasonable grounds, that it was.

attributes.value: This party says that Foodstuffs owns three grocery brands, limiting competition on prices in NZ. Instead of Foodstuffs being divided into North and South Island branches, the company should be divided into New World and Four Square and Pak 'n' Save, creating greater competition.

attributes.value: This party would amend the Grocery Industry Competition Act in its first 100 days in government, asking the Commerce Commission to develop an implementation plan for separating the businesses in a way that is good for consumers. Owner-operators of supermarkets would retain their roles, but with a different overarching company structure to get support from. Restructuring Foodstuffs is a faster way to reach three competitors in the New Zealand market, rather than the time it would take for another player to develop operations around the country.

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that it should be easier for large commercial projects to be built in New Zealand without needing a council inspection. Making it possible for engineers to sign off on parts of projects will reduce council inspections for parts of construction. Council capacity could be dedicated to consents and management of housing, and mean large projects could be built more quickly and cheaply.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would allow qualified engineers to sign off on building work by clarifying the role of producer statements in the Building Act, giving these descriptions a standard role in consent processes. It would also create a dedicated dedicated Building Consent Authority for large commercial projects, with specialist expertise and a nationally consistent pathway for consents. Developers could choose to use this BCA or get approval from their local council.

attributes.value: This party says that older New Zealanders need the balance in relationships with retirement village companies to shift more towards residents. attributes.value: This party would require retirement villages to pay residents or their families 10 percent of their net termination proceeds within four weeks of when they leave a unit. It would retain the current "hardship pathway" and current exit protections for residents, like stopping weekly fees when a occupation agreement ends. attributes.value: This party says that affordable and reliable power is essential for growing the economy. Currently, those with solar panels are locked into selling any excess power to the grid to the same company they have an electricity contract with. attributes.value: This party would give every household and. business the right to sell power to whichever retailer they choose. International trials have found that low-dose CT scans for people at high risk reduce lung cancer deaths by 20 to 25 per cent.

attributes.value: This party says that Jobseeker benefits are not meant as long-term support. The current "invest to save" programme should be continued and extended, with work support targeted to people who have been receiving a benefit for a longer period of time. More intense case management and employment programmes should be used to target the problems preventing people from being employed, and younger people should particularly receive more help. This will help to balance the welfare system more effectively.

attributes.value: This party would target extra case management and employment programmes to people receiving Jobseeker benefits for over 12 months, who are deemed "job-ready". At least 5,000 of these places would be reserved for young people. An additional $12m would be given to youth work programme He Poutama Rangatahi above existing baselines. It is estimated that this programme would save $9m by 2031.

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that welfare support should always be temporary, and after a long time receiving a benefit it is hard for people to find work. While the welfare system should provide a safety net, it should not prevent people from seeking work. Decreasing payments for people who have been receiving benefits for more than two years will incentivise these people to seek work. Parents with dependent children would have their payments decreased less than those without children.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would reduce payments for people who have been receiving Jobseeker benefits for 2 of the last 3 years, even if these periods of support were not consecutive. From April 2028, this party would reduce the rate for single people to the rate for 20-24 year olds; reduce the rate for couples without children, and reduce the Jobseeker rate for parents with dependent children half as much as for those without. The exact reductions would be based on benefit rates in 2028, as the rate changes with inflation. The Supported Living payment would not change. This party estimates this would save $572m over 4 years.

attributes.value: This party says that the intention of Jobseeker benefits is to help people find work, not to provide long-term support. Many types of work require drug tests for workers, so people receiving Jobseeker benefits should also be tested for drugs, to show that they are ready to work. If drug use is a barrier to employment, it should be addressed.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would institute random drug tests for people on Jobseeker benefits, as part of MSD's broader employment programme. If drugs are detected, a person will be tested again; if drugs are detected again, MSD will conduct a mandatory assessment to see whether drug use is a barrier to employment and whether it should be addressed. If drug use if not addressed, it could result in benefit sanctions, so that payments are reduced or stopped. It is expected that this policy would cost $1.5m per year.

attributes.value: This party says that employment disputes can be expensive and time-consuming, even if a dispute is relatively minor. attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would work with schools to align the start and end dates of the school year to make these dates more consistent.

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that the Hauraki Gulf is a special area and "Auckland's playground". It believes that the waters of the Gulf are best used by people who fish, dive, swim, or collect kaimoana recreationally. Further protection for the Gulf will preserve these recreational uses.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would establish the Hākaimangō-Matiatia Marine Reserve off Waiheke Island as a 23 square km marine reserve, and expand the size of the existing Goat Island marine reserve. It would remove the exemption for ringnet fishing in the High Protection Areas of the Gulf. The current ban on collecting shellfish and other species from rockpools would be maintained and this party would impose higher penalties and enforce this ban more strictly. It would develop a Sustainable Fisheries Plan for the Hauraki Gulf by consulting with industry, including reviewing the current corridors where bottom trawling is allowed.

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that at least 600,000 New Zealanders go fishing occasionally, and recreational fish provides food and enjoyment, as well as supporting the business of charter boat tourism for fishing access. Fish stocks need to be maintained for recreational users, but fishing for food is a right and should not require a licence. This party says that honorary Fisheries Officers, who do enforcement work on a voluntary basis, could be doing more of the work of fisheries enforcement.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would ensure that no licence is required for sea fishing. It would ban the commercial sale of marlin, so hunting this fish can continue to be a sport. Enforcement and fines for people who do not obey catch limits would be increased, and part of this enforcement would be carried out by increasing the number of Honorary Fisheries Officers to 200 around the country. There would be some instant fines for people who catch more than the limit of fish.

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that New Zealand has over 1900 seamounts (mountains and hills on the ocean floor which often have more biodiversity) in its Exclusive Economic Zone (the area of ocean which a country has the right to resources within). Protecting these areas is important, as is following the Crown's obligations under the Fisheries Settlement of Te Tiriti. It says better data can protect this area while also maintaining access for recreational and commercial fishing.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would increase protection in the EEZ, aiming to increase from 32% of protection in the EEZ currently to 50% by 2040. It would prioritise protecting seamounts and vulnerable species like coral. More broadly, this party would continue to uphold the government's obligations to protect fisheries under Te Tiriti o Waitangi.

attributes.value: This party says that the fishing industry is worth nearly $2bn and supports many jobs in NZ. Technology can increase the efficiency of the industry, for instance new designs that reduce how many seabirds are caught by boats. This party wants to support the seafood industry to invest by matching its investments in new technology.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would match investment in new technology from the seafood industry, up to a total of $10m, to create a $20m fund in total. The focus would be on equipment that reduces seabed contact and bycatch.

attributes.value: This party says that NZ's fishery laws needs to be fit for purpose and a changing climate. A committee needs to examine and test all aspects of a proposed Fisheries Amendment to ensure reform is fair for all interest groups.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would balance commercial and recreational interests in any reforms to fisheries law. It says that improving the current Quota Management System would be a focus of reform and transparent data about fish stocks and how many fish are being taken would be prioritised too.

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that fish stocks move across international boundaries and into the high seas, so international cooperation is required to manage fish. The High Seas Treaty, also known as the Agreement on Biodiversity Beyond National Jurisdiction (BBNJ), came into force on 17 January 2026. It can be used to regulate marine genetics, assess environmental impact of fishing and set up marine protection areas outside of national jurisdictions. While NZ has signed the treaty it has not ratified it by bringing it into NZ law.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would ratify the High Seas Treaty on international fisheries and biodiversity.

attributes.value: This party says that most land in NZ is privately owned, including areas which have high biodiversity or significant natural features. The QEII National Trust is a voluntary mechanism where landowners can create covenants to preserve land. This party says that there is growing demand for assessments from the Trust and secure, permanent funding will increase the impact of the Trust.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would increase the QEII Trust's annual funding from the current level of $4.2m to $8.5m per year. This increase would be confirmed in the 2027 Budget.

attributes.value: This party says that young New Zealanders who have moved overseas should have a reason to return, stay, and work and live in NZ. Within 100 days of being elected, this party would institute a range of policies aimed at New Zealanders thinking of returning. Particularly, it would focus on people who have met their partners overseas, so it is easy to return to NZ with their partners.

attributes.value: This party would prioritise and expedite work and visitor visas for partners of NZ citizens.

policies.statement: Expedite work and visitor visas for the partners of NZ citizens

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that some people are concerned about housing growth impacting their streets, such as an increase in cars trying to park on the streets. Previously, the minimum requirement for the number of carparks in new housing was removed, but this party says the result has been roads clogged with cars and parking on berms and footpaths.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would remove the ban on having any minimum parking requirements set by councils for new house developments. Instead, it would allow councils to use minimum car parking requirements in suburban areas outside those identified for intensification, such as around rapid transit stops and city centres.

attributes.value: This party says that many Aucklanders spend too much time sitting in traffic or waiting for delayed trains. Removing level crossings in Auckland increases safety on the Auckland train network for trains and cars, and means the frequency of trains can be increased.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would progress with level crossing removals in South and East Auckland as part of rail network upgrades following the City Rail Link.

attributes.value: This party says that Aucklanders spend too much time sitting in traffic, which is bad for families and for businesses. The Eastern Busway is an already-underway project to increase the frequency of buses in East Auckland, so that public transport is faster and more reliable for people in this part of the city.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would complete the Eastern Busway bus route to Botany from Auckland's city centre.

attributes.value: This party says that parts of Auckland are growing rapidly, and require more space in classrooms as the school roll grows. This party says that there are 727 new classrooms funded across Auckland and these should be finished, as well as wanting to build a new school in Drury in the south of Auckland.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would deliver 499 approved classrooms across Auckland, 203 of which are under construction and 296 of which need to be completed. It would also progress the Drury Specialist School for high-needs kids, aiming to open by Term 1 in 2028. It would secure the Drury East primary school site for a future school in this area.

attributes.value: This party says that health services need to be planned as communities grow for the decades ahead. A site for a new hospital has been approved in Drury, a new housing development in the south of Auckland, and this party wants that hospital to be built.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would progress the building of a new hospital in Drury, south of Auckland. A 13 hectare site has already been secured for the hospital.

attributes.value: This party says that NZ's agriculture workforce is getting older; the average farmer is now 58. There need to be more young people working in the agriculture sector, and providing more school options for people interested in these subjects is one way to create this outcome.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would introduce an industry led "food and fibre" subject into the curriculum, which students could take in Years 12 and 13. The subject would start in 2029.

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that the average farmer is 58 years old, and the agriculture workforce is getting older. This party wants more young people to come into this industry, particularly emphasising how much of NZ's agriculture gets exported. Landcorp, the government-owned company which owns farms throughout NZ, already has schemes to encourage young people which this party wants to expand.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would expand Landcorp's apprenticeship scheme, which offers young people farming experience and qualifications while working. It would also grow Landcorp's farming equity schemes for dairy and livestock, which are a way for younger farmers to build equity while working towards owning their own farms. This party also supports an already-announced $10,000 scholarship for "future leaders" in agriculture and horticulture.

attributes.value: This party says that a survey of 192 people working in regional health services said a lack of diagnostic tools and cardiac imaging was a major unmet need for delivering health services. This party wants to connect diagnostic tools in public and private hospitals and use mobile scanners so that people needing healthcare can get it more quickly.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would roll out mobile diagnostic services in rural areas of NZ. It would also link diagnostic tools in public and private hospitals so the tools that already exist can be used to their maximum capacity. It would report results and lengths of wait times so there is transparency about what is happening with this important issue.

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that the arrival of H5N1, the very pathogenic avian influenza, is one example of how NZ agriculture is threatened by biosecurity breaches. This party wants to increase visitors to New Zealand and trade with other country, which also creates risks for biosecurity. It wants to pass new legislation to protect the agriculture industry from unwanted pests and diseases as much as possible.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would increase penalties for serious biosecurity breaches from $1000 to $2000 and grant biosecurity officers the right to refuse entry or deport people holding temporary visas. It would pass an amended Biosecurity Act and amendments to the Hazardous Substances and New Organisms Act to strengthen the biosecurity system and increase access to agricultural and horticultural products and veterinary medicines from overseas.

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that it is a party of low tax, and pricing emissions through the Emissions Trading Scheme is a type of tax. While other industries must be part of the ETS, it says that NZ farmers should not have to follow this, and technological solutions should be able to reduce emissions rather than pricing systems. It says it supports the international Paris Agreement to reduce emissions, but that emissions reduction should not be achieved through pricing agricultural emissions.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would continue to exempt agricultural emissions, including methane, from the ETS. It also supports a different way of calculating methane emissions where current levels of emissions are maintained.

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that NZ uses over 2 million tonnes of fertiliser every year. This fertiliser grows grass, which feeds cows and sheep, which are exported as meat and milk. Fertiliser is created from imported phosphate and processed in NZ, which makes NZ vulnerable to price changes in the international phosphate market. This party wants to use diplomatic efforts to ensure that NZ has a continuous supply of fertiliser.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would negotiate fertiliser security arrangements with key phosphate-supplying countries, modelled on an agreement with Singapore on essential supplies. It would also create a $10m "Critical Agri Inputs" fund to invest in fertiliser production and distribution, in partnership wit the industry. This money would come from the Primary Sector Growth Fund.

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that many of NZ's young vet's are moving to other countries, which is a problem for the agriculture industry. The number of places in Massey University's vet training programme is increasing by 15 students from 2027, and this party also wants to increase the number of students who can sign up for the voluntary bonding scheme, which provides a financial incentive to new vets who commit to working in rural areas for a time after graduating.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would double the vet bonding scheme to 70 places each year from the 2027 funding round. The scheme would also be open to NZ citizens and permanent residents who have trained in accredited Australian vet schools and are qualified to work in NZ. There would be reporting on results from the scheme each year, an a full review after three years. This party estimates that this would cost $2m each year once fully implemented, with the money coming from MPI baseline funding.

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that the "right to silence" is a fundamental part of the judicial system where people can choose not to speak in a court case if they do not wish to. However, citing high-profile examples of children who have been killed while adults who were present refused to give information to authorities, this party says it wants to penalise people who do not speak when there are investigations of the death of a child.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would impose a maximum penalty of 10 years imprisonment for people who choose not to give information regarding the death of a child. It would apply when a child under the age of 12 dies and it is unequivocal that an adult was present. This party would amend the Crimes Act, in consultation with legal experts, to create this change.

attributes.value: This party says that it can be difficult for older people to navigate government systems and access what they're entitled to. Creating a single helpline will make it easier for people to get help.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would create 0800 SENIORS, a number senior citizens can call for help with government services and support. The helpline will sit within MSD and be funded from existing baselines.

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that a current 'granny flat' policy has made it easier to build affordable, warm, safe homes for older people. This party says these rules should be expanded to apply to more small dwellings, including tiny houses and attached garages. It says older people deserve affordable and quality housing.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would allow attached garages to be consented under the 'granny flat rules' for houses up to 70 metres squared. Tiny homes on wheels would also be allowed to access these rules. This party would require PIM (project information memorandums) to be processed within 5 working days and keep fees to cost recovery. The requirement for a primary dwelling would be removed. This party would also explore a new licensing class for builders working on this type of building to ensure that homes are built with high quality standards.

attributes.name: Why
attributes.value: This party says that not all old people can or want to live in retirement villages. This party says that 15 percent of people on the Housing Register are older than 65 and a third are 55 or older, meaning that many old people do not have secure housing. The Housing Flexible Fund is a contestable housing fund from the government for different kinds of affordable housing solutions, and this party says that some of that should be focused on housing for older people.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would ringfence 20 percent of Housing Flexible Fund dwellings for older people. Social homes, affordable rentals and other types of housing will all qualify.

attributes.value: This party says that seniors' savings and security should be protected. Many people choose to keep working after the age of 65 and these people should still get employer contributions to their Kiwisaver.

attributes.name: How
attributes.value: This party would require employers to continue Kiwisaver contributions for employees over the age of 65. This change would begin on 1 July 2027.

attributes.value: This party would review the Enduring Powers of Attorney Framework (which allows people to choose trusted others to act on their behalf if they cannot make decisions), and consider further law changes to protect seniors from economic harm.
